title: Outdoor temperature sensor fault
shortDescription: The condenser unit's ambient temperature sensor is open or out of range.
fullDescription:
On Armstrong Air variable-capacity (4SCU16LX/SLX) condensers, E1 indicates the outdoor temperature thermistor is open, shorted, or reads outside the -40 F to 150 F window. The control board substitutes a default value, which causes inefficient operation and may inhibit cooling at extreme outdoor temperatures.

Most common causes are rodent damage to the sensor pigtail, water intrusion into the sensor connector, or a sensor that simply aged out. Replacement is a 15-minute job once the sensor is sourced.
safetyWarning: Lock out the disconnect at the outdoor unit before opening the control panel - 240 VAC is present near the contactor.
symptoms: E1 on indoor display or fault LED

fixSteps.title: Disconnect outdoor power
fixSteps.instruction: Pull the outdoor disconnect and verify zero volts before opening the panel.

fixSteps.title: Locate sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Find the small thermistor clipped to the outside of the coil with a 2-pin connector to the control board.

fixSteps.title: Measure resistance
fixSteps.instruction: Compare to chart - typical 10K NTC at 77 F. Open or very high reading = replace.

fixSteps.title: Replace sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Plug new sensor in, route away from sharp edges, restore power.

whenToCallPro: If the new sensor still produces E1, the control board input may be damaged.

faq.q: Will the AC still cool with E1?
faq.a: Yes, but on default backup logic - efficiency and protection features are degraded.

title: Coil temperature sensor fault
shortDescription: Outdoor coil sensor open or out of range, blocking variable-speed control.
fullDescription:
E2 reports the outdoor coil thermistor as open, shorted, or wildly inconsistent with ambient. The communicating board uses this sensor to manage defrost timing on heat pumps and to set superheat targets on variable-speed compressors. With E2 active, the unit may run at fixed capacity or refuse to start.

The sensor is typically a 10K NTC clipped to a U-bend in the coil. Vibration over time can break the lead, especially near the strain relief.
safetyWarning: 240 VAC at contactor and capacitor, plus residual capacitor charge after disconnect. Discharge capacitor with a resistor before working near it.

causes.cause: Broken thermistor lead at strain relief

symptoms: Heat pump fails to defrost properly

fixSteps.title: Power off + verify
fixSteps.instruction: Pull disconnect, confirm 0 V at contactor line side.

fixSteps.title: Inspect sensor mounting
fixSteps.instruction: Verify the thermistor is firmly clipped to the coil tube. Re-seat if loose.

fixSteps.title: Continuity test
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect sensor plug; ohm both leads. Open = replace.

whenToCallPro: If sensor checks good, control board input is suspect - tech replacement.

faq.q: Where is the coil sensor located?
faq.a: On Armstrong communicating units, clipped to a return-bend on the lower section of the outdoor coil.

title: High pressure switch trip
shortDescription: The high-side refrigerant pressure exceeded the safety cutout (typically 600 psi R-410A).
fullDescription:
E3 indicates the manual or auto-reset high-pressure switch on the discharge line opened. On R-410A units this typically corresponds to roughly 600 psi. The compressor stops immediately to protect against rupture.

Leading causes are dirty / blocked outdoor coil, failed condenser fan motor, restricted air path due to debris or shrubs, an overcharged system, or a stuck-shut TXV. Repeated E3 events should be diagnosed before resetting - a damaged compressor is the alternative.
safetyWarning: High-pressure refrigerant can cause frostbite and eye injury. Refrigerant work requires EPA 608 certification.

causes.cause: Failed condenser fan motor or capacitor

symptoms: Hot air not blowing through condenser

fixSteps.title: Wash condenser coil
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect power, gently rinse coil from inside out with garden hose - no pressure washer.

fixSteps.title: Verify fan operation
fixSteps.instruction: On a cooling call, the condenser fan should run any time the compressor runs.

fixSteps.title: Test fan capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: After discharging, measure capacitor uF rating. Out of spec by >6% = replace.

fixSteps.title: Pressure check
fixSteps.instruction: Have a tech gauge the system and verify subcool/superheat targets.

whenToCallPro: Refrigerant adjustment, TXV, and compressor work all require a licensed HVAC tech.

faq.q: Can I just keep resetting and running?
faq.a: No - repeated trips can damage the compressor and indicate a real problem.

title: Low pressure / loss of charge
shortDescription: Suction pressure dropped below the cutout, indicating low refrigerant or restriction.
fullDescription:
E4 means the low-pressure switch opened, typically below 50 psi on R-410A. The IFC stops the compressor to prevent ingestion of liquid refrigerant or starvation damage.

Common causes: refrigerant leak (Schrader cap, evaporator coil, line set), severely dirty indoor coil or filter starving airflow over the evaporator, failed indoor blower, or operation at very low ambient (below 60 F) without low-ambient kit.
safetyWarning: Refrigerant leaks displace oxygen in confined spaces and can produce toxic phosgene if exposed to flame. Ventilate and avoid flames.
symptoms: Frost on suction line or coil

fixSteps.title: Replace filter
fixSteps.instruction: Install a clean filter and run blower-only to thaw any ice on the indoor coil (1-2 hours).

fixSteps.title: Verify service valves
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm both stem caps removed and valves are fully back-seated open.

fixSteps.title: Leak search
fixSteps.instruction: Tech inspects with electronic detector or UV dye - pay attention to evaporator and Schrader cores.

fixSteps.title: Recover, repair, weigh-in charge
fixSteps.instruction: Tech repairs leak, evacuates to 500 microns, and weighs in factory charge per nameplate.

faq.q: Is topping off charge a real fix?
faq.a: No. EPA forbids it without leak repair, and the leak will return.

title: Compressor over-current
shortDescription: The inverter or contactor saw current draw above the compressor's safe limit.
fullDescription:
E5 indicates the compressor drew current above its rated locked-rotor or running threshold. On variable-capacity Armstrong Air units this is detected by the inverter; on single-stage units, by an external CT or thermal overload.

Most common causes are a seized or stiff compressor (especially after a long off-season), failed run capacitor producing low torque, low line voltage, or refrigerant overcharge.
safetyWarning: Repeated over-current trips can damage windings. Do not jumper the overload to keep the unit running.

fixSteps.title: Discharge and test capacitor
fixSteps.instruction: After power-off, short capacitor terminals through a resistor, then measure uF.

fixSteps.title: Verify line voltage under load
fixSteps.instruction: Measure L1-L2 voltage during start attempt. Should stay above 207 VAC.

fixSteps.title: Inspect lugs and contactor
fixSteps.instruction: Look for pitting and discoloration. Replace contactor if pitted.

fixSteps.title: Hard-start kit (last resort)
fixSteps.instruction: If capacitor and voltage are good, a tech may add a hard-start kit to assist a tired compressor.

whenToCallPro: Compressor replacement requires recovery, brazing, evacuation, and weigh-in charge.

faq.a: The instantaneous current at startup. Compressors briefly draw 4-7x running amps.

title: Communication loss between indoor and outdoor
shortDescription: The communicating bus between the air handler/furnace and condenser dropped out.
fullDescription:
E6 appears on Armstrong Air communicating systems (Comfort Sync) when the i+, i-, R, and C bus fails to maintain valid handshake packets. The system reverts to non-communicating logic where possible.

Causes: reversed i+ / i- wiring at one end, broken thermostat wire (rodents, lawn aeration), water in the buried whip, or a failed control board on either end.
safetyWarning: Low-voltage but ensure the 24 VAC transformer fuse hasn't blown - shorted communication wires can blow it.

causes.cause: i+ and i- swapped at outdoor unit
Failed comm IC on control board

fixSteps.title: Verify wiring color
fixSteps.instruction: Confirm i+ to i+ and i- to i- (not swapped) at both indoor and outdoor terminals.

fixSteps.title: Inspect outdoor connector
fixSteps.instruction: Open whip and check for water intrusion or corrosion.

fixSteps.title: Continuity test wires
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect both ends; verify no shorts between conductors and full continuity end-to-end.

whenToCallPro: Replacing buried thermostat cable usually requires a tech with a fish tape.

faq.q: Can I run the system with E6?
faq.a: Yes, on default fixed-capacity logic, but you lose efficiency and dehumidification benefits.

title: Indoor blower fault
shortDescription: The indoor air handler reports the blower is not running at the commanded RPM.
fullDescription:
E7 in cooling mode means the outdoor unit got an OK to run but the indoor blower is not at the commanded RPM. ECM blowers report tach feedback to the control board; if the actual RPM is more than 200 RPM off target for 60 seconds, E7 sets and the cooling call is suspended to prevent coil freeze.

Causes include a failed ECM module, a stuck or shorted blower wheel, dirty filter starving airflow, or a broken tach wire between the motor and control board.
safetyWarning: Blower start may be sudden after fault clears. Keep hands clear of the blower wheel.
symptoms: Cooling stops while outdoor unit is OK

fixSteps.title: Replace filter
fixSteps.instruction: Install clean filter, allow any coil ice to thaw with blower-only operation.

fixSteps.title: Spin blower wheel by hand
fixSteps.instruction: Power off; the wheel should spin freely with minimal axial play.

fixSteps.title: Check motor harness
fixSteps.instruction: Verify all 5-pin connectors fully seated and look for chafed insulation.

fixSteps.title: ECM swap
fixSteps.instruction: If wheel is free and harness intact, replace ECM module per service bulletin.

whenToCallPro: ECM motor diagnosis and replacement is best done by a technician.

faq.q: Can a dirty filter actually freeze the coil?
faq.a: Yes - low airflow drops coil temperature below freezing and ice forms within an hour.

title: Discharge line over-temperature
shortDescription: Compressor discharge temperature exceeded the safety threshold (typically 270 F).
fullDescription:
E8 indicates the discharge thermistor read above the safety setpoint. Sustained high discharge temperature breaks down compressor oil and damages the windings. The system shuts the compressor down for a 5-minute cool-off then retries.

Causes: low refrigerant charge, restricted liquid line / drier, dirty indoor or outdoor coil, or a compressor with a damaged valve plate. On variable-capacity inverters the algorithm may also trip if outdoor temperature is extreme.
safetyWarning: Refrigerant work requires EPA certification. Hot discharge line can cause severe burns - allow 30 minutes to cool.
symptoms: Discharge line very hot to touch

fixSteps.title: Wash outdoor coil
fixSteps.instruction: Power off; rinse coil from inside-out, gently.

fixSteps.title: Verify discharge sensor
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect; resistance should match chart at room temp (typically 50K NTC).

fixSteps.title: Have charge verified
fixSteps.instruction: Tech checks subcool/superheat and compares to nameplate.

whenToCallPro: Always for refrigerant or compressor work.

faq.a: Normal is 150-200 F. Above 250 F is dangerous and triggers E8.

title: Inverter / drive board fault
shortDescription: The variable-speed compressor drive reported an internal fault (IGBT, DC bus, or temperature).
fullDescription:
E9 is a generic inverter fault on Armstrong Air SLX and Comfort Sync units. The drive's protection circuits detected one of: IGBT over-temperature, DC bus over/undervoltage, output ground fault, or drive heatsink over-temp.

This is rarely a DIY fix. Drives are sealed assemblies replaced as a unit. Outside causes (poor airflow over the drive heatsink, loose lugs, failed line filter) should be ruled out before replacing.
safetyWarning: DC bus capacitors hold lethal charge for 5+ minutes after disconnect. Verify zero volts before touching any power components.

causes.cause: Loose lug or damaged line filter

symptoms: Sometimes accompanied by an audible click then silence

fixSteps.title: Power off + wait 5 min
fixSteps.instruction: Pull disconnect, wait at least 5 minutes for DC bus to discharge, verify with multimeter.

fixSteps.title: Clean drive heatsink
fixSteps.instruction: Vacuum dust from heatsink fins and verify cooling fan operation.

fixSteps.title: Inspect lugs
fixSteps.instruction: Torque-check all power lugs to spec. Burned lugs need replacement.

fixSteps.title: Drive replacement
fixSteps.instruction: If fault persists, drive assembly replacement by a tech.

whenToCallPro: For any drive replacement, refrigerant adjustment, or compressor work.

faq.a: Most Armstrong Air variable-capacity units have 10-year parts warranty when registered.

title: Reversing valve fault (heat pump only)
shortDescription: The reversing valve failed to shift between heating and cooling modes.
fullDescription:
On Armstrong Air heat pump variants, E10 indicates the system commanded a reversing valve change but the discharge / suction temperature pattern did not match expectations. The valve may be stuck mid-stroke, the solenoid coil may be open, or the pilot bleed port may be plugged.

This is a common code after extended idle in shoulder seasons; sometimes a single full cycle of cooling-then-heating frees a stuck valve.
safetyWarning: Reversing valve replacement requires recovery and brazing - not a DIY repair.
symptoms: Heat pump runs but blows wrong-temperature air

fixSteps.title: Test solenoid coil
fixSteps.instruction: Disconnect plug; ohm coil. Should be 30-200 ohms typical. Open = replace coil only.

fixSteps.title: Force a mode swap
fixSteps.instruction: From thermostat, alternate between cooling and heating to attempt to free a slightly-stuck slide.

fixSteps.title: Tech replacement
fixSteps.instruction: If coil is good and slide is stuck, a tech recovers refrigerant and replaces the valve body.

faq.q: Why does my heat pump blow cold in heating?
faq.a: The reversing valve didn't shift - exactly what E10 catches.
